core.title: State the file's one job in a Purpose: line of at most 80 characters
core.given: Any implementation (non-test) file in the codebase
core.when: its header is authored, changed, or checked
core.then: The header carries a single `Purpose:` line of at most 80 characters that truthfully names the file's one job.
prefer: During GREEN, derive the purpose from the responsibility introduced for the current acceptance.
Use concrete responsibility language rather than implementation mechanics.
If the purpose genuinely cannot fit because the new file owns multiple jobs, split only the responsibilities required by the current behavior.
avoid: Inventing a vague purpose just to meet the length cap.
Unrelated decomposition: when splitting a file whose purpose does not fit, do not decompose anything beyond the responsibilities the current behavior requires.
unless: The file is a test file (test files are excluded).
core.why: An unbounded description becomes a paragraph that goes stale and, being believed, is worse than none; the 80-character cap forces naming one job, and a purpose that will not fit usually signals a file doing more than one thing (a design signal as much as a documentation rule).
evidence: The convention check reports no missing or over-length `Purpose:` finding for the file.
Reviewer confirms the purpose truthfully names one job and fits the limit.
verification: A validator-style check covers every implementation (non-test) file in the codebase, whether new, edited or unchanged, and reports a finding when the header's `Purpose:` line is missing or is 81 or more characters long.
The length cap is inclusive: exactly 80 characters passes; 81 does not.
A missing `Purpose:` description is reported at the header's URN line; the concrete anchor follows the stack's header identification idiom.

Test files are excluded from the check; the exact classification of files as implementation versus test belongs to the stack's realization (its checker), and this core asserts no particular identification mechanism.
Severity 2; disposition strict: the check fails on every finding, with no advisory mode and no ratchet baseline.

fires: A new implementation file is created without a `Purpose:` line in its header.
An existing, unchanged implementation file has no `Purpose:` line when the codebase is checked.
An implementation file's `Purpose:` line is 81 or more characters long.
An implementation file's header has a URN line but no `Purpose:` description (reported at the URN line).
doesNotFire: A test file has no `Purpose:` line (test files are excluded).
An implementation file's `Purpose:` line is exactly 80 characters.

bunOnly.reason: Detector, validator and finding ids of this one rule are realization details; the core's verification describes the check generically, and other stacks find the same obligation through their own detectors.

neutralityNotes: The obligation itself is already stack-neutral (bun.json's own activation note says so); the only Bun-specific content is the detector/finding identification in verifier_detail[3]. The `Purpose:` label and the 80-character cap are constants of the shared cross-stack obligation (the source's core alias is shared by the Bun, Python and Vite realizations), so they remain in the core rather than becoming profile data. bun.json states no concrete suffixes, paths, comment syntax or URN syntax: it defers the implementation-versus-test file classification and the header/anchor syntax to its own checker. Because bun.json supplies no authoritative values for any vocabulary key, profileRequirements is empty and the checker-owned classification deference is kept in core:verification instead of being represented as absent profile data. The 'reported at the URN line' anchor assumes the stack's header idiom carries a URN line; a stack without one would anchor the missing-description finding at its own header identification line. 'Detector' in evidence[0] was generalized to 'the convention check'.
